utterances.text: And, sir, while that's being called up, it may take a few moments, can I ask you when you used the word "communication," were you referring to communication lines travelling through Rajlovac or were you referring to something other than that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about going via Rajlovac or travelling via Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you -- maybe if we could -- well, first, before I zoom in on anything, can I ask you whether you would be able to indicate Rajlovac on this map in its current projection? Without doing -- without touching, just tell me yes or no because I want to know whether I need to have it zoomed in or not. Would you be able to indicate Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you to put a dot and next to it put an R to indicate the location Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to put a dot and the Latin letters H and Q to indicate where your headquarters or the headquarters of the Ilidza Brigade was.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you -- okay. I can see a dot. But can I ask you to put the letters HQ next to that so we'll know that that indicates "headquarters."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, it looks like there's an H and a K there for headquarters. The Prosecution would tender this as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Page 65 of Exhibit P3 as marked by the witness receives number P6613, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's me ask you this: It would appear that Rajlovac would be the way out of --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was confused by the blue lines. In our system of markings we use red for our forces and blue for enemy forces. This seems to be a map of the Army of BH because the numbers are -- the colours are in the other -- the wrong order. Before I mark anything, could I get a chance to have a closer look at the map in order to eliminate any potential mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure. And can I ask you this: Does this mean what you've just said that we should vacate that last exhibit and start again?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We need to remove my markings because I was confused by the separation lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll vacate the exhibit that we just admitted and we re-start this whole exercise. And, Mr. Groome, I would suggest that we then zoom in on what seems to be here the numbers 5, 6, 9, 10, and 13, 14 which gives a detail of that part of town and the Chamber knows where that is in relation to the whole of the city. Madam Registrar, the number vacated is now P66 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 6613, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 13. And we re-start here. Perhaps we zoom in first on the quadrants 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14. Like that, yes. Witness, this is not a map of any army but it is a map which was produced for the -- for the Tribunal. Now in order to give you some guidance and if the parties disagree, please let me know immediately, the red dotted line indicates the -- where the positions at the front line for the BiH army were, whereas the blue dotted line indicates the VRS side of those same confrontation lines. And I think we should then also re-start that you mark again Rajlovac. Mr. Groome, could you take over here --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and ask the witness to again mark Rajlovac to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Colonel Radojcic, before you make any other markings I just want to confirm that you now have -- having looked at the map you are able to orient yourself and you can accurately locate Rajlovac for us.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can mark Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Again a dot and the letter R.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I see the letter R. Is that right over the location of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dot represents the central part of Rajlovac, the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I see that now. Now could you do the same thing for your headquarters. Put a dot and the letters H and Q.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can indicate my command post on this map. We would need to go further to the left in order to be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So can you help us by saying to the left of which of these quadrants, 5, 9 or 13 would your headquarters be located?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the left of quadrant 9. It would be to the left of quadrants 9 and 13. Those would be the quadrants I would focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, could I now tendered this version of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map now marked with Rajlovac, not yet with the headquarters, that now replaces P6613. Madam Registrar, could you confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That would be number P6613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, this would appear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, of course, is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what I meant by replacing. But since we had vacated it, there's nothing to replace. It is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, the path between your headquarters and Rajlovac would be going in a northerly direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you drew the outer ring --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's now P6612.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And we can bring it up if you want to see it. Am I correct in understanding your markings there that there was also a southerly way that you could leave your -- your headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One couldn't go south because the only exit in order to communicate between Ilidza and Vogosca went via Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just let me take a look at paragraph 4. I didn't recall that it was between Ilidza and Vogosca. Now, so paragraph 5 - I'm sorry, it's paragraph 5 - it doesn't say the only communication between -- between the brigade and Vogosca. It says the only communication our brigade had with the rest of Republika Srpska was through Rajlovac. So now my question is: Could you not have gone in a southerly direction from your headquarters and reach other parts of the Republika Srpska through that gap in the outer ring that you indicated on P6612?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no roads which could be used for motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your evidence is that you could not go. Despite the fact that there was a gap in the outer ring, your evidence is that you could not traverse the area where that gap was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I understand now. Now, in paragraph 7 of your Mladic statement, you say that one objective of the VRS operations around Sarajevo was to block the main force of ABiH 1st Corps from leaving Sarajevo and being utilised on other fronts; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it looks as if you are now entering a new --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I do see that it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we should take the break now. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. If there's any need for Mr. Mladic to have a closer look at the map, that can be arranged during the break. We take that break and we'll resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be brought in. The Chamber was informed that Mr. Mladic had an opportunity to look at the map and where the pins were during the break. Mr. Groome, will you further examine the witness on the southerly link with -- through the southerly route from Rajlovac or from the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I may tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I need to do a bit of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one other matter that relates to the pins. While examining it, the one of the pins did become dislodged from the map and fall to the ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- which I gave to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So I wanted to put that on the record that I did not want to reinsert it because I honestly did not see that there were pins there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my follow-up report was that Madam Registrar returned the pin to Mr. Groome and that Mr. Groome said that he would not use the map any further and that therefore the removal of the pin had no significance for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm glad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to before we move on just perhaps take stock of where we are now so far in your examination. It seems that you acknowledge that evidence that would be important in this case has been removed from the statement tendered in this case. It seems that you now acknowledge that your evidence about a double encirclement is not factually accurate. So what I want to ask you is, is it a case that these are honest mistakes on your part or have you come here to give biased evidence in an effort to help Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I really came with honest intentions, to tell the truth. As for that problem that we had with the terms of "encirclement" and "semi-encirclement," if you can find my statement given to President Karadzic I think that it is the term "semi-encirclement" that is used there. I would kindly ask you to do that in order to resolve this dilemma. I was in -- at the military academy I was a professor of tactics, and I really doubt that I could have used the word "encirclement" instead of semi-encirclement. So I can only attribute this to an unintentional mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, I have a copy of that statement in your language. I'll ask the usher to give it to you, but I ask you not to look at it now. During the next break take a look at it, and the first question I'll ask you when we return is to show us where the term "semi-encirclement" is used, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, could I ask the witness be provided a copy of his Karadzic statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then be it given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I was beginning to talk to you at the break about paragraph 8, and there you talk about the impact of the 1st Corps breaking the blockade of Sarajevo and you say the following: "If the BH Army 1st Corps broke out of the Muslim-controlled city of Sarajevo, it would have had a major effect on the other fronts and the course of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina because those forces would be used on other fronts." My question is: Is it your view that the ABiH needed the 1st Corps troops blockaded in Sarajevo on other fronts?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they also knew what the objectives were, political and military of the Serb side, towards Sarajevo, during the second part of the war they tried to get the main forces of the 1st Army of BiH out of Sarajevo and to use them at different fronts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I correct in understanding your evidence that it is quite possible or you believed that had the 1st Corps been able to leave Sarajevo such an event would have resulted or could have resulted in a different outcome to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it would lead to a different outcome of the conflict, I'm not sure. But that it would have affected other parts of the front line, that I am sure of. Because a mass of 40- or 50.000 armed men is certainly relevant in terms of affecting the outcome at certain parts of the theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if we look back at paragraph 4 of your statement, you say in reference to the 45.000 to 100.000 troops in the 1st Corps: "As needed, the forces were manoeuvred out of the city and vice versa. This manoeuvring was carried out through a tunnel dug under the airport runway or across the runway at night." Is it your evidence that the ABiH was able to move troops in and out of Sarajevo at will?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And one of the ways that they did this was through a tunnel that was 1 to 2 metres diameter?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the soldiers would have to go through that tunnel or come into that tunnel in a single file; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then the other way was to run across the airport runway, a path that left them exposed to SRK fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your experience or your estimation, how many troops would have come in or gone out on a daily basis of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very hard to give a precise answer to that question because the soldiers left town going to Igman and coming back when there were changes at positions. They did not carry weapons then. They left weapons at Mount Igman and returned without weapons so that it would be easier for them to go back. How many people came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please focus on the answer, whether it was with or without weapons. Mr. Groome asked you to tell us from your experience or by an estimation that how many troops that could have -- would have come in and out on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I wanted to say. If they carry all their weapons and their full combat kit, then it is much more difficult to get through. The very fact that they did not carry these weapons shows that more soldiers managed to get out and come back at a given point in time. What the exact number would be, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But let's take it one by one, Mr. Groome, if you wouldn't mind. The tunnel. How many troops would you get through the tunnel of 1 or 2 metres, as Mr. Groome put it to you and you did not challenge, to go through that tunnel on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the interpreter made a mistake. Not 1 to 2 millimetres but 1 to 2 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is must be somewhere some confusion, but I think everyone is talking about metres. But, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly the width and the height of the tunnel limits the number of people who can get through that tunnel. I assume that during one night or during the course of one day, but they mostly used it at night because they were exposed to our activity in certain parts, they would manage to get one or two companies through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A company consisting of how many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's say the average size of a company was 150 men, so during one day between 250 and 300 men could have been transferred without any problem whatsoever without stopping the flow of goods --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because we have to know that in this tunnel goods were also being transported and even civilians who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from the goods, how would people move through that tunnel which must have been of considerable length? Did they crawl, did they -- was there any carriage on rails? What was it that how they could get through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never entered the tunnel. What I'm saying, I'm saying on the basis of conversations with persons who did move through that tunnel. As far as I know, people have -- had to bend forward in order to get through. Also, they had the problem of negotiating parts of the tunnel where there was lots of water and where there was a shortage of oxygen. So it was not easy to get through this tunnel at all. On the basis of statements made by witnesses or rather persons who went through that tunnel, and I talked to them, that's what they said. I think that they also used rail to transport goods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they used rail, do you know how many carriages there were driving over that rail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, just a few minutes ago when talking about the military since of all the troops blocked in Sarajevo, you said that -- that they were certainly relevant in terms of affecting the outcome at certain parts of the theatre of war. So it seems that it would have been important to be able to get those troops out, if possible. Then you've also said that those troops could be moved in and out of Sarajevo at will. Now you've just said that it was not easy to get through that tunnel. My question to you at this point is: You're not being exactly precise when you say that they were able to move forces in and out of the city as needed. That's not exactly precise, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "as needed," I meant, first of all, that they transfer these people when they were changing their soldiers at Igman. Let me go back to that erroneous term, the external ring. So when they exchanged these shifts, it was done through this tunnel. Now the remaining people that they would get out in order to involve them at other parts of the front line, I don't have any specific information, but using military logic I can infer that I would use them at different front lines, because the Sarajevo front was under a lot of monitoring of the monitors, of the world public, et cetera, so it was obvious that the Serb side did not want to resolve the question of Sarajevo by military means. That is why they needed to get these soldiers out of Sarajevo. 75.000 as far as I know. That is their information. The 1st Corps had 75.000 mean. This is a major human potential, and it would be a pity for it to remain untapped in Sarajevo whereas there is combat going on elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, if they needed to get these troops out that had tremendous potential for assisting them in other parts, if what you say is true, that they can move them in and out as needed, do you know why they didn't? Why didn't them simply take 40.000, move them out, send them to another front? Do you know why they didn't?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't do that probably because they were preparing throughout the war to deblockade the 1st Corps. They tried that twice, the last time in 1995, and they succeeded in getting the main force --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the corps out of Sarajevo and -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- why would they need to break the blockade of the corps if what you're saying is true, that they can move in and out as needed? Why did they need to break the blockade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in that way they would have opened a wide area through which their forces could leave rather than having those problems already referred to in terms of leaving through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to move onto another topic. Paragraph 9 of your statement you say in the second sentence of that paragraph: "Minor offensive actions were carried out at the beginning of the war before the lines of defence stabilized and during the war outside of the corps's zone on the order of the superior command; for example, in the Nisici Plateau area and in Operation Lukavac." So my question is: Is the reference to Operation Lukavac a reference to Operation Lukavac 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now the Chamber has recently heard evidence about Operation Lukavac, how it involved the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, how it involved the Herzegovina Corps, and its ambitious aims with respect to territory. Why do you characterise the operation as "a minor offensive action"? Why do you do that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the role of the members of my brigade in those operations was a minor one. The number of people involved in operation Lukavac under the command of General Galic ranged, say, well, it was around 350 men. In my statement, what I meant was activities based on the decision of the brigade commander; that is to say, when they took part in operations within the area of responsibility of the brigade. I meant not in larger scale operations than.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, you remember what I just read, and I won't read that again. I'll read you the sentence before that, paragraph 9: "The SRK and my brigade executed primarily defensive actions and went on the offensive in the corps' area of responsibility only in the initial stage of the war in order to improve tactical positions." Sir, you were referring to the entire corps, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the Ilidza Brigade and the participation of my units within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, when we did take part in these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So do you wish to change your evidence about whether or not Lukavac 93 was a minor offensive operation, or do you still maintain that it was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that it was a minor operation. On the contrary, it was a major operation, a strategic operation, operative strategic operation. So it would be absurd for me to claim it was a minor operation. No. My forces took part in small operations such as, et cetera, I mentioned Lukavac. But we did take part but we were not a decisive factor in that fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness's statement, D535, be brought to our screens and that we go to paragraph 9 in both. I believe it's e-court page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you have a hard copy of your statement, so you can get a look at it a bit quicker than us. Take a read of paragraph 9, then I'm going to ask my question again. So, sir, you've just said Lukavac 93 was a major operation. Am I wrong in reading it here that you've described it as a minor offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must have misunderstood it. If you allow me, I'm going to read out the statement and explain what the mistake is. Could you please return the previous page for me because I don't have that portion here right now. Please do enlarge it a bit. Thank you. This is what I say in my statement: "In the beginning of the war before the lines of defence were stabilized, minor offensive actions were carried out and during the war outside the corps's area of responsibility on the order of the superior command; for example, in Nisici Plateau area and in Operation Lukavac." The very name Operation Lukavac shows how big it is because in military theory, operation, battle, that is the highest category of combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, to say that we should deduce from the name that is called operation that where you said it was a minor offensive action we should understand that to be a major offensive action is -- requires quite a lot from our flexibility, because the text clearly refers to minor offensive actions and then refers to Operation Lukavac as one of them. Now to say we should understand from the word "operation" that it wasn't minor, then at least you put a puzzle before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second part of the sentence reads: "... and during the war outside of the corps's zone on orders of the superior command," that is to say, minor offensive actions do not pertain to actions outside the zone of the corps. It just means what we did within the area of responsibility of the brigade. I thought that if I used the word "operacija," operation, in Igman that that automatically means how big it is. There are three categories of size. There is battle; there is combat; there is operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. You say we may have misunderstood it, but your evidence is that your involvement may have been rather limited but that Operation Lukavac was a major military operation. Is that your evidence? Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, it seems --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It seems that every time I ask you about some specific text in your statement, it's not what it appears on its face to be. Before I proceed, are there any other portions of your statement that you need to correct, that you need to say you're not sure about, or that you need to tell us -- you need to interpret it in a particular way to really understand what I'm really trying to say. Is there anything else you want to tell us about your statement before I continue asking you questions about it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't change anything, not even in this text that you find controversial. I thought that if I say "operacija," operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that is carried out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- by operative forces and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you were not invited to revisit the matter we had just dealt with. Mr. Groome asked you whether any other portion in the statement would need further clarification, correction, guidance in understanding it. That was the question. Anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can respond that I don't know what it is that the gentleman, the Prosecutor, will not find comprehensible. That is why I am here to give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say I'm not aware of any other portion where, as far as you can imagine, a further explanation would be needed. Then, Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to change the topic now. In paragraph 26, you speak of a number of topics including the fact that you sent regular combat reports. Okay? Sir, just to avoid confusion can I ask you to take the Karadzic statement which is to your right and turn it face down. We will have an awful lot of confusion if you start referring to that statement here. Just put that face down. That's the one that the usher just gave you. Flip it over. We're not going to use that now today -- or not at the moment. The Mladic statement is to your let, the one that you received yesterday. And I'm directing you to paragraph 26? You say in reference to combat activity: "I kept the superior command informed of all such instances by sending regular and interim combat reports." Now the Chamber has heard detailed evidence about the VRS system of daily written and oral reports. I'm not asking you to go into that now. My question is simply whether you sent regular and interim combat reports on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for regular reports, yes; whereas, interim reports were sent as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, was there ever a time in your tenure from -- from the beginning of 1993 to the end of the conflict that you were unable to send a report to your superior command because of something that was happening in the battle-field or some other reason? Was there ever an occasion that you can remember that you were unable to send a daily report?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I exclude that possibility. The reports were sent daily. If I was not there, a report would be sent by my deputy. It was the task of the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you provide honest and complete reports of the activities of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that was my duty. It would have been a crime if I had decided to misinform my superior command and I would have been liable for that, if I had decided to misrepresent the situation in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Apart from misrepresenting, did you have to report on unsuccessful tasks; that is, you were asked to do something and your brigade was unable to achieve success in the task? Were you obliged to report that to your superiors as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if you were asked to target, let's say, a mortar position at a particular location and you attempted to do that but you missed it, would that be something that you would have to report to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was asked to destroy a target, I would have followed through. It never happened to me that I received a task and I didn't complete it. There was no need, therefore, to report on a failed mission, especially if that mission was a combat mission. There were some tasks I didn't complete, but those were never combat tasks. When it comes to combat task, I always strived to complete them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the question theoretically. Let's say there was a lesser commander than yourself who did fail in a task, would that commander be obliged to report the missed target or the failure to his superiors in his daily report?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your reports, did you provide honest and complete reports of enemy activity in your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if your superiors read your reports, they would know in detail what soldiers in the Ilidza Brigade were doing and what was going on within the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can draw your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome could I ask for one clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier questions were put to you in relation to targeting with mortars an object, and part of your answer was, well, it was -- if it was combat activity, you never failed to achieve what you had to do. Do you consider launching a mortar projectiles to a target, would you consider that to be combat activity or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, that would have been a combat activity. Whenever you use combat assets and live ammunition, you were in combat and such an activity is considered a combat activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you engaged a target with mortar fire, you said you never failed to -- it haven't -- "it never happened to me that I received a task and I didn't complete it." So that would be true then for such a -- for engaging a target with mortars as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I have to say that brigade artillery was under my direct command, 76-millimetre cannons; 105- and 122- howitzers; whereas 120-millimetre mortars were in battalions; whereas 82- and 60-millimetre artillery weapons were part of the company. So if I had been given a task to use mortar and destroy a target, I would have done it very successfully. I must say that mortars are less precise as a combat asset than the artillery tools that I had at my disposal in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you would follow up and achieve your task anyhow, even if, due to the imprecision, initially you would have failed to hit the target, is it, because you said we would not give up until we had done our task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that in my previous answer. My artillery was deployed at places from which we had optical visibility with all the targets that were given as targets to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all nice. But you told us that you never failed to fulfil a task, especially when it was combat activity, and you confirmed that engaging a target with artillery would be such a task you never failed to perform. That is how I understood your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if -- and you hinted at the lack of precision of mortars, for example, then even if the first projectile didn't hit the target, then, as you told us, you would perform the task anyhow, so I take it that you would then do that by the second or the third or the fourth shot. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that also mean that if an artillery projectile falls at a certain location, which is -- well, let's say, near - you hear interpretation? Yes - which is near to what you considered to be a military target and if there's no follow-up hitting that military target, that then apparently what was hit must have been the target. You understand what I mean? Because if where the projectile landed was not the target, you told us that you'd never failed to perform your task and then hit the target with one of the next projectiles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now turn to the topic of modified air bombs, and you gave extensive evidence about that yesterday. I want to break down my examination into different particular aspects, so I'm going to ask you as best you're able to focus on the particular aspect that I'm dealing with at the time, and the first aspect is the destructive power of the modified air bomb. Now I want to read you an excerpt from your Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for Ms. Stewart's benefit, I'm on page 17. I'm jumping a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to read you an excerpt from your Karadzic testimony and ask you whether you stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is the Karadzic case at transcript 31249.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is the question you were asked and the answer you gave: "What kind of destructive -- actually, the destructive power of these bombs, 100 and 250 kilos, is massive; correct? "A. When we say contact-fuse aerial bombs weighing 100 kilos, we have to know that the explosive charge accounts for 40 per cent of the total weight of the bomb. The rest is the body of the aerial bomb. And that after the explosion during which the bomb is fragmented, of course this is massive. Yes, it's a powerful bomb." Do you stand by that evidence that you gave before the Karadzic Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that the destructive power you are referring to is the destructive power of the air bomb. You're not giving any consideration to the rocket's destructive power. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to read you a description of the destructive use and capacity of these air bombs that we found in a technical document of the ABiH Army which also possessed aerial bombs. I want to ask you whether you agree with this technical description. "The contact-fuse high impact aerial bomb is a classic highly destructive aerial bomb intended for the destruction of facilities of medium and large resistance, these being command centre buildings, shelters, bunkers, bridges, railroad junctions." Would you agree with this technical description of the capability of an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record can we have the exhibit number that Mr. Groome is quoting from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The ERN number is Y0145122, Y0145128.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, what document number is that on the 65 ter list for cross-examination that was provided to the Defence for use with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic is correct. It is not on the -- the document list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should have been, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was disclosed to the Defence, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it's not, I can do that, Your Honour. That's my error. I apologise to Mr. Ivetic for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it now and then happens. We should try to avoid that it happens too often. As a matter of fact, try to avoid it to happen at all. Mr. Ivetic, if you need further time for that to have a look at it, but it might have not have done with the witness today, so therefore if you need more time, then please tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to return to your Karadzic testimony. When you said: "... of course, this is massive. Yes it's a powerful bomb," you were referring to a 100-kilo bomb. Am I correct that a 250-kilo air bomb would be approximately or have approximately two and a half times greater destructive capacity than a 100-kilo air bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly more destructive. But that doesn't mean that a 250-kilo weighing bomb has 40 per cent. The correct technical information would be 35 to 40 per cent. I can't give you a more precise answer as to how much more destructive would a 250-kilo-weighing bomb be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now this quarter-of-a-tonne bomb, there weren't many bombs with greater destructive, were there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the armament of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're right. There weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you have seen the destructive capacity of a 250-kilo air bomb personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had that opportunity. If needed, I can repeat its basic parameters that illustrate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. I want to ask you a question that perhaps will help illustrate the destructive capacity. You have been to this court building several times. If a 250-kilo air bomb were to be dropped directly on this building, would it destroy the building?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What percentage of the building would you say would be destroyed, if it suffered a direct hit from a 250-kilo air bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we're talking about contact-fuse air bomb, the principle of its action is this: The ignition has a retardation, it is adjustable, and it will all depend on how thick the obstacle is. The purpose of its use is not to destroy and demolish but to pierce and then there is a detonation whose impact destroys everything on its way. This doesn't mean that it would demolish the whole building. It only means that once it fell into the building, its kinetic energy would create a huge pressure which would then destroy both the assets and the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So again my question is: What percentage of the building would be destroyed in the way you described if a single 250-kilo air bomb had a direct hit on this building?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would destroy the entire wing on which it fell. So if it was adjusted to destroy only the top floor, it would destroy the roof and the top floor and it would damage everything below it. If the retardation was higher, then it would go deeper. It would destroy the floor onto which it fell and it would damage all around it. It would depend on the material, whether it is reinforced concrete or some other material resistant to the effect of an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you've used a term which we're having difficulty or the interpreters are having difficulty interpreting and it's what is adjusted. I think you mean that what is adjusted is the time between the contact with the fuse and the time of the actual detonation of the bomb. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primer is made in such a way that the explosion can be adjusted to one, two, or three seconds from the moment the bomb hits a building. So when you set that time, the bomb will go on piercing through the building until the moment it is activated and it is activated or the time is set by you. There is deceleration depending on the target and the material it's built from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now yesterday you described three aerial bombs that you were personally involved with. Do you recall what the fuse was set to in each of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer because I don't know. My chief of artillery did that with the crew, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to turn -- now I want to focus simply on the rockets that are used to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome can I ask one matter for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You started with -- talking about 100-kilogram bomb which would, as you said, contain 40 per cent of its weight for explosive material. And then Mr. Groome took you to the 250-kilo bomb. And then you said, well, that doesn't mean that they have 40 per cent. The correct technical information would be 35 to 40 per cent of weight found in the explosive materials. I was puzzled by that answer and I'll tell you why. Usually if you take a larger container then the weight and the material used for the container itself, if you make it bigger, becomes proportionally less than the volume you gain inside that container. Do you agree with that? If you have a small bottle, then the glass is taking relatively more of the weight of the filled bottle than if you have a larger bottle. Would you agree with that? Now, why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see you're nodding -- you're nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now why would that be different with a bomb? If you make it larger, then I would expect the proportion of the volume where the explosive is found to be higher rather than lower, similar as a larger bottle containing more fluid relatively compared to a smaller bottle. Could you explain to me why you nevertheless when talking about a heavier, a larger bomb would take it that the explosive material would be less in percentage compared to a smaller one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the encyclopedias that I studied and from which I learned, there is information according to which aerial bombs contain 35 to 40 per cent of their total weight, so I can't give you a precise answer. I can't talk about a 105-millimetre bomb and tell you whether it's 40 kilograms or 35 kilograms because the literature that I studied does not give a definition of that kind. However, logic follows your thought and makes me think that you're right in saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were first asked about a 100-kilos bomb and you were -- your testimony was put to you whether the explosive charge accounts for 40 per cent of the total weight of the bomb and then you said you stood by that evidence. You didn't say it's wrong, "In encyclopedia I read that it was 35 to 40." But when talking about larger bombs, you said it doesn't mean that it's 40. It could be anything between 35 and 40. It could be anything 45 and 45, which was missing logic for me. And you've tried to explain that. But your first answer was that you stood by the 40 per cent that was read out to you as your previous testimony. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but -- I said that, but that would have been an average value, between 35 and 40. That's why I said 40 per cent. And I agree totally with the way you are thinking, which is that logic could lead us to a weight of 250 kilograms for a bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking is because you start at 40 per cent. We're talking about larger bombs and you are reducing the explosive power, more or less, by saying it was 35 to 40 per cent, not necessarily 40 per cent. Whereas, my logic would tell me that the explosive power would increase, and perhaps considerably increase, and you agree with the logic of that. So I'm puzzled by why in your answers you go down in explosive power, relatively, whereas you agree the logic telling you that it should go up. That's the reason why I asked you those questions. If you want to comment on it, please do so. Otherwise, we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just wanted to be more precise, and I said that that's -- that was 35 to 40 per cent. Perhaps this aerial bomb has 45 per cent. I'm not saying this is correct or not. I wanted to be more precise which is why I offered an average or a median value of 35 to 40 per cent. It was not my intention to reduce its explosive power in any way because it a powerful asset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock. We are one or two minutes from a point where we would take a break. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be fine to take the break now, Your Honour. And I would just say that Ms. Stewart has graciously uploaded that document we were speaking about. It's now under 65 ter 30874 should Mr. Ivetic and the Chamber wish to take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Could the witness be escorted out the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes, Witness, and we'd like to see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. 30 minutes. Half past.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness if I could correct a misstatement that I made on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In reference to that document, which is 30874, I have incorrectly characterised it as the ABiH assessment of its own air bomb. What is, in fact, is the ABiH's Army assessment of the air bombs which were -- held by the VRS. So it's their assessment of VRS weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I remember well, but I'm also looking at you, Mr. Ivetic, the portion that was read, that the meaning of it was not influenced as a matter of fact by whom was commenting on -- on whose equipment, so therefore I'm just looking at you as well to see whether we can leave it to what Mr. Groome just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's my recollection of the part that was cited as well. But again, the provenance of a document is always necessary to be known what -- what the scientific value of the same is or what the weight attributed to it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's -- but that's a matter which is apart from the question that was put to the witness where it was just a quote which was given. Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Radojcic I want to focus on Plamen rockets and that component of a modified aerial bomb. Now, in your Karadzic testimony at T31251 you state: "We used rockets that were used by the Plamen multi-rocket-launcher. They were used as the fuelling agent." Do you stand behind that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not completely. Later on I found out that there is a Grom variant. I'm not sure. Believe me, I'm an infantry officer. I spoke about this. I said that there were some rockets, but it is possible now there are Grom-type and Plamen-type. So my statement in that regard was perhaps not fully correct. Also the number. I mentioned four then, but later on I found out that it was three, as in three engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ivetic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to enquire: During the Prosecution's case in-chief when we were presenting prior testimony, it was our obligation to upload the same in e-court and have it up on the screen so that everyone could follow. It's my understanding that this transcript is number 30850 on the Prosecution's list, and I'm wondering why we're not following the same procedure. I have a paper copy and am able to get to it, but it does take me some time to locate the page numbers when the Defence had an obligation to put it up on the screen. So I'm just wondering what Your Honours' guidance on that would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I think there are two issues. The one is to have the prior statement on the screen if you want to present that as evidence, and at the same time the Chamber guided the Prosecution not to introduce under Rule 92 ter portions of the previous statement by the -- by the witness. So there may be some confusion about what now should guide the Prosecution. But I think there's nothing wrong on having and even would preferable to even if a portion of a previous testimony is put to the witness to have that portion on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because I recall Your Honour specifically wanted the context of what was before and after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. I think if we could have 65 ter 30850 or does Ms. Stewart have -- Ms. Stewart has it available. If we could put it on the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's in e-court -- 65 ter 30850 and it's on e-court page 44, line 24. Okay. So the Chamber will be able to look at that, Mr. Ivetic will be able to look at that. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've made these qualifications to that prior testimony, and my question in follow-up to that is: Of the three air bombs that you say you fired from your brigade, were they all Plamen rockets or did they have a combination of Plamen rockets and Grom rockets as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all of them were Plamen. Later on I read in literature that Grom was used too, but I think it's Plamen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So as far as you're personal knowledge about the weapons that were sent up from your brigade, they were all Plamen rockets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm a bit puzzled by the phrase "they were used as the fuelling agent." Witness, do I have to understand this as they were used as the propelling agent or -- I have some difficulty in understanding how rockets can be fuel or fuelling agents, whereas I could understand that rockets are propelling agents for the bomb if attached to that bomb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. The fuse is on the top and it is activated as I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there may be now another confusion between fuses and fuelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to go through in tremendous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- detail all the different components. Perhaps it might assist the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- to let me do that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Colonel Radojcic, I want to tell you my understanding of a Plamen multi-rocket-launcher and then ask you to either correct me or say that I have it right. Now, I understand that a Plamen multi-rocket-launcher consists of 32 128-millimetre rockets that can be fired in rapid succession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now my information is that they could be set to fire these 32 rockets in -- anywhere between six seconds to roughly 20 seconds. Does that sound roughly accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your agreement is not recorded, sir, if you nod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is correct but I would kindly ask you to bear in mind that these questions are way too professional for me. These are questions for an artillery officer, whereas I'm an infantry officer. Perhaps these are even questions for an expert. So I kindly ask you to ask me questions about things that you assume that I may know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I appreciate that you're assisting us and this is not your field of expertise, but to the extent you are able to tell us that you roughly know or that certainly is helpful. These rockets are launched from a special launcher that sometimes is -- is mounted to the back of a trailer or a large vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this launcher has tubes; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, 32 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the rocket is aimed by calibrating the elevation angle as well as the bearing of those tubes; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a range finder and also -- I mean, that is for setting the distance and the elevation. And you've been referring to the azimuth and that means actually setting the angle. So we're basically referring to the same thing, artillery protractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just to be clear, there are two adjustments - one up and down, and the other laterally - to aim those tubes; correct? Again we need to have you say something to be recorded on the record.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And they have a range of about 8 kilometres; is that correct? Or if you know.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the -- the designed usage of the Plamen rocket system is to suddenly and very significantly attack front line troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One multiple rocket-launcher, when it is fired fully, it covers 300, 400 metres, by 300, 400 metres. So that is a platoon, as far as defence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I correct in thinking that the tubes are not aimed individually but the entire casing that holds the 32 tubes is -- is manoeuvred in order to aim the rockets? Again, we would need you to ...

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If a single rocket were to land on an average-sized home that we may all have seen in the Sarajevo area, would it have the destructive capacity to destroy that home?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the fuse of a multiple rocket-launcher acts momentarily. It is quite different than that of an air bomb. So the very instant when it touches the surface it is activated and that is why it is intended for destroying manpower, personnel, as opposed to air bombs. We've already discussed that, what that is used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now prior to launching the Plamen rockets, they're all loaded into the tubes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if an entire salvo is being fired. Sometimes only five or ten rockets are being fired. But if it's an entire salvo within the time-frame that you referred to, then all rockets are placed in tubes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that when the rocket engine ignites, the projectile is forced out of the tube in a path controlled by the tube?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's analogous to a bullet being placed in the chamber of a long-barrelled weapon and being fired. The path of the barrel controls the path of the bullet; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Shall I give the reasons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you can do that without hinting at the content of the testimony but just in legal terms, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Calls for speculation and asserts matters not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before deciding on the objection, is there any dispute between the parties that barrels of weapons, especially if they are longer, are designed to guide the projectile to the aimed target?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that there's not a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is -- there is a distinction, and I don't want to go into technical terms, but I would not say that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll rule on the -- Mr. Groome, you are invited to put the question in such a way that -- and always to find out first what the witness's knowledge about technical aspects is. And then on every and each matter the Chamber will consider whether or not, if the witness has difficulties in answering the question, whether we would allow you to proceed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, according to your statement you were an instructor both in the VRS Military Academy and then also in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the air force academy in Rajlovac until the beginning of the war. But my unit was relocated to Belgrade when the war started. And then I was transferred to the Military Academy for Land Forces, and I taught one semester there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now based on being an instructor and based on being a brigade commander, do you feel yourself competent to be able to give me an answer to a question which asks whether the path of a bullet is controlled by the barrel it travels down?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then can you please answer that question. Does it in fact control --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we want to be more accurate in this answer, perhaps it's better to compare a mortar barrel to the barrel of a multiple rocket-launcher, because a mortar can have a barrel of 60-millimetres, 82-millimetres, 120-millimetres, et cetera. The barrel is lowered and then it is fired and ballistics laws are in play just like in the case of Plamen except that the trajectories are different between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I agree with you --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I agree with you that perhaps is the better example, so do I understand correctly that the tube of a mortar functions -- well, let me reverse it, please. The tube of the Plamen rocket-launcher functions very much as the tube of a mortar. It aims the path that the projectile will take.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now the individual rockets do not have guidance systems; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by guidance systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They don't have the same technology that maybe a Tomahawk missile would have that would carry it to a specific location. The tube is simply aimed and the rocket is fired; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And it is based on the rules of ballistics. So they have a ballistic trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And each individual rocket has its own individual warhead; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct that when a rocket fires from the launcher, the launcher vibrates in response to the force of the rocket igniting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't call that vibration. We call it trigger. But that happens after the rocket leaves the tube. So that moment when it leaves the tube, the rocket, I mean. I think that it is Newton's third law, that is when this happened, but that is once the rocket has left the tube and that is why it does not affect precision otherwise it would be catastrophic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that why the rockets, although they fire in quick succession, they don't fire simultaneously, to allow that trigger effect to settle before the next rocket is fired?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that is the case. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the Plamen rocket system is not designed to fire rockets simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that they can all be fired at the same time. I mean, in the same second. There has to be a certain time interval involved, as you mentioned at the outset. I think it was six seconds or something like that. At least that's what I observed. And I don't think I ever saw anything different. I think that would be an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now want to focus on the air bomb itself. And we've heard from you yesterday that the 250-kilo air bomb was designed as a weapon to be dropped from overhead by a plane flying over its target; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has no independent propulsion system; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has no guidance system; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It hits its target by the force of gravity and the accuracy is determined by when it is dropped and from how high; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to shift to building the air bomb, the modified air bomb. Now, to create a modified air bomb, a rocket -- or multiple rockets were attached to either a 100-kilo or a 250-kilo air bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many rockets would be attached to a 100-kilo air bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have them in my brigade, but as far as I know one rocket would have sufficed to propel such a bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many would be attached to a 250-kilo bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would be three Plamen rockets in the context of your experience?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now would you agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I seek clarification. About the 100-kilo. You said as far as you know, did you say one rocket would have sufficient power to propel such a bomb or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did not have those bombs, but I believe that it was launched with only one rocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree with me that rockets were attached to the air bombs using two general methods. The first one was to screw the rocket into the back of the air bomb itself?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I did not inspect that at close range but it is possible. I'm not sure. I don't know how it was attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. The other way of attaching, which I believe is the way that was done in your brigade, was to use a welded frame to attach the rockets around the outside of the air bomb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my previous answer, I can't answer because I did not inspect those bombs. When they were launched, I would be standing some 20 to 30 metres away from them and I did not really inspect them at close range.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know if when they were attached that they were attached with their warheads intact?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can't touch it. It's full of TNT. You can't remove it and then return it. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now yesterday you told us that the Ilidza Brigade built its own launchers. My first question in this regard is: How many launchers did you build?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We built one launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And yesterday at transcript 23044 you said: "Rocket-launchers were manufactured by us based on sketches we received from our superior command. The basis -- or the base was actually a truck with a back that could be lifted up and down." My question to you is: Did your superior command specify the type of truck that needed to be used?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we used the trucks that had a hydraulic lifting mechanism that already existed and created an elevation. I don't think that they prescribed the make of lorries. There was an expert team in Energoinvest, which was a company, a team of engineers. They were provided with drawings and they dealt with that. I don't know anything about that, but I know that a team of top-notch experts were gathered round that problem in order to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did your superior command provide with you any specialised parts to make the launcher or was it simply the drawings and that materials that could you acquire locally could be manufactured to create the launcher?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used drawings and then a manufacturer would find appropriate materials and proceeded to craft such a launcher based on the sketches provided to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So there were no specialised parts that were provided from the superior command, just the drawings?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset, I said that that was not my primary task. I had my assistant for logistics who dealt with that issue. I just received reports informing me that we received bombs and a launcher. That's what I was concerned with. The technology, the crafting of the launcher and the bombs was within the purview of my assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what the track was made or what the rails that the -- the bomb would -- would lift off? Do you know what that was made of?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were rails on the launcher. I don't know how the rails were lifted, what kind of mechanism was used to elevate them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you now look at a video of a rocket and a rocket-launcher. We'll -- according to the practice in this trial that we've been following, we'll play it twice to ensure the accuracy of the interpretation or the language on the video. After the second time that it's played, I'll ask you some questions about it, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 22344.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So we'll now watch it one more time and we should, at least those of who don't speak Serbian, B/C/S, will hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voice-over] "21st Sabotage Detachment has invented, realised, and demonstrated in practice the use of artillery for sabotage purposes. 21st Sabotage Detachment was the first to use a mobile rocket-launcher in combat "Go. "The exceptional strength of the detachment's fire-power is shown by the possibility to launch 18 250-kilo bombs in a one 5-second burst of fire as well as 152, 57-millimetre rockets."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I have a few questions to follow up on this. The air bombs that we see in this video, do you recognise them as either being 250 kilo or 100 kilo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that what we saw were 100-kilo bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand your evidence, you did not have this specific type of modified aerial bomb in the Ilidza Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We didn't have either bombs or a launcher of this kind to launch them. I believe that we saw five launching pads. We only had one. This is actually the first time I've seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would the launcher that you had, recognising it only had one set of rails, would it operate according to the same principles generally that we've seen here on this video?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the principle would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 22344.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object. The witness has not authenticated that such a launcher was known to him, that he has knowledge of how it operates, or that he had it in his possession. So we still don't know -- the foundation for this video has not been laid by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply offer it to -- the witness has said that it demonstrates the similar principles as the launcher that he used. There are not a lot of videos of rocket-launchers in use, so I believe it does have relevance for this Chamber's determination of facts related to air bombs, and on that basis I tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The witness testified as to what he saw on the screen was operating in a way similar to what he experienced within his own brigade with his aerial bombs. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number still has to be' signed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22344 receives number P6614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
